title: The Nest
text:
It is because a little mountain bird has made,

in the hollow of a tree, its morning nest,

that the tree dawns with music in its breast,

as if it had a musical heart.


If the sweet little bird peeps through the hollow,

to drink dew, to drink aroma,

the tree of the hills gives me the feeling

that its heart has come out, singing.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the tree's nest as an exposed singing heart.

title: White Clothes
text:
On the threshold of the hut stands María;

the shadows of her eyes are rivals

of those shadows the coffee groves give

when day begins to fall asleep...


She is a girl who dreams and raves,

if one speaks to her of the lad with the shawls,

and she shells corn into aprons

and scents the nearness with love...


When at the river she spreads white clothes

—beside the pool where the water stands—

under the love of the hut's moon,


the white clothes pretend, from nearby

hills, to be a band of doves

pecking at stars in the river...
editorial_note: The translation keeps the white laundry becoming doves at the river.

title: The Parakeets Pass
text:
The afternoon wakes from its dream,

when the wing-light cloud begins singing...

A cloud of wings... a joyful cloud that descends, that rises...


It is they. They move away between plain and sky.

They are the emeralds of a necklace in flight...


Noisily they trace a green curve in the air,

Are they going to the palm groves of waving fan?

They go wherever their beaks point them.

They move away, they move away... but they go so together,

that rather they seem lines of dots...


And they fall in a plain,

as when a tree is shedding its leaves.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the parakeets as a winged green necklace and then a falling tree.

title: Quezaltepec
text:
The night was Dantesque... In the midst of muteness

suddenly broke the rumbling of thunder...

A troop of colts that had broken the bit

and hurled itself, untamed, into the abyss...


A pale glare of cataclysm,

the sky that before had shown itself serene,

sinisterly illuminated in full,

as if the sky itself were burning...


Amid a thousand convulsions of mountain

the red and throbbing entrail opened

on that bitter night of hardship...


And from the crater in the open wound

burst the burning lava, enraged,

like a boa burning with lust.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the volcanic sonnet's dramatic animal force.

title: As the Coyol Flower Half-Opens
text:
I feel a vague childish tenderness

when in the coolness of the damp orchards

the sweet cicadas of April weep

their unsayable uncertain prayers.


Trembling cries that the subtle breeze

carries on its wings, like dead leaves

toward the soft plains, open

beneath skies of rose and indigo...


Oh, singers of the laughing hut,

who with their tenderness lull the river

as the coyol flower half-opens...


And in their songs they sigh and weep

among the clear groves gilded by

the melancholy sunsets...
editorial_note: The translation keeps the cicadas as singers of the hut and the coyol flower's half-opening.

title: The Turtle-Dove
text:
Coo-coo, coo-coo! Are you moaning,

turtle-dove of the rice field?

Look, you are doing me

much harm with your song!


Coo-coo, coo-coo! The hamlet

is filling with calm,

and an orange tree and a palm

are kissing in the river...!


Little pitcher filling yourself

with the water of the stream:

How beautiful it is to look at the sky

beneath serene afternoons!


Field lily, dark-skinned girl

who smells of milk and roses:

How happy the soul is

when life is serene...!


Among rosy fineries

the afternoon falls asleep.

Turtle-dove that is moaning:

You are a madrigal with wings!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the songlike exclamations and the rural tenderness of the original.

title: Tree of Fire
text:
So vivid are the blushes

of your flowers, rare friend,

that to your flowers I say:

"Hearts made into flowers."


And at times I come to think:

If this tree became lips...

ah, how many kisses would be born

from so many lips of fire...!


Friend: what lovely garments

the Lord has given you;

he preferred you with his love

dressed in cloud-colors...


How good heaven has been to you,

tree of my land...

With my soul I bless you,

because you give me your poetry...


Beneath a garden of cloud-colors,

seeing you I came to believe

that the sun was already sinking

inside your branches.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the fire tree's flowers as hearts, lips, and sunset.

title: Cane Field in Bloom
text:
The cane fields were seas

that I contemplated one day

(my boat of fantasy

rowed upon those seas).


The cane field is not garlanded

like seas, with foams;

its flowers are rather feathers

on emerald swords...


The winds —perverse children—

descend from the mountains,

and are heard among the canes

as if stripping verses of leaves...


While man is unfaithful,

so good are the cane fields,

because though they have daggers,

they let their honey be stolen...


And how sad the milling

though through the estate flies

the troop of joy,

because mills and canes

shatter entrails...

They pour tears of honey!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the cane field's sweetness, violence, and honey-tears.

title: The Pale Little Girl
text:
That pale little girl who lived

begging alms, from inn to inn,

was found on the threshold at daybreak,

with little hands stiff and heart mute.


No one knows who she was or where she came from;

her laughter was a grimace of disillusion.

And the bitter seal of melancholy

was perpetuated in two deep charcoal circles.


On human flesh hunger left its traces...

The clouds looked at her, the stars knew it...

The sky rained stars in the peace of the suburb


No one knows who the pale little girl was...

Meanwhile —in the night, the sad warm night—

dragging stars, the turbid stream goes on...
editorial_note: The translation keeps the elegiac anonymity and the stream dragging stars through the night.

title: The Colts
text:
The colts are already drawing near; swiftly

the group defines its contours of wild beauty;

through the pale rose of the languid landscape

they run unbridled, level with the breeze.


The colts are drawing near: but they do it so fast,

that they seem to fly over the quiet place;

their hooves move in a fantastic journey,

leaving behind huts of imprecise silhouette.


Hurricane-like over the native plains,

the fugitive colts go devouring leagues,

to mock the efforts of useless pursuit;


like a winged shadow they pass before us,

and the sturdy farmhands, fleeing after the colts,

draw flourishes in the wind with their lassos...
editorial_note: The translation keeps the galloping visual energy and the lassos writing in the air.
